item.title: [CBS News World] China launches first foreign astronaut to its space station
item.description:
China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station.
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.
Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.
Astronauts Muhammad Zeeshan Ali of Pakistan and China's Wu Yi and Tang Hongbo wave at a send-off ceremony on Nov. 25, 2026.
Andy Wong/AP Photo
The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, official Chinese news agency Xinhua earlier reported. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space," he said on X on Tuesday.
The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.
While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.

Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.ByRachel ClunBusiness reporterPublished24 November 2026Updated 1 hour ago
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.
During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

item.description:
Officials are searching for a man who went overboard during a cruise vacation on board Royal Caribbean's Allure of the Seas, according to Bahamian officials.
The Allure of the Seas is on an eight-day Thanksgiving cruise in the Caribbean that departed from Miami on Sunday.
The cruise line called out a passenger's name over the ship's loudspeaker system for several hours before determining that the man had gone overboard, according to passengers on board the cruise ship. The ship then turned around to look for him, the passengers said.
The ship's captain announced Monday that the crew had "received a report of a missing guest" earlier in the day before determining "that the guest had unfortunately gone overboard," according to two recordings of a captain's announcement obtained by CBS News.
Christian Bunse, a passenger aboard the ship, told CBS Miami, "People got quiet when they heard it, because they heard his name again."
Royal Caribbean told CBS News that it "immediately launched a search and rescue effort" to find the man and are working with authorities.
The Coast Guard said the Allure of the Seas alerted it and the Royal Bahamian Defense Force of a man overboard at around 11:30 p.m. on Monday. The Coast Guard said the man was reported to have gone overboard off the coast of San Salvador Island, Bahamas. The Royal Bahamian Defense Force is leading search efforts for the man, aided by the Coast Guard.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

item.description:
The Picture Show
How tariffs, fuel and fertilizer costs are squeezing the U.S.'s biggest apple region
November 24, 20264:09 PM ET
By
Anna King
Loading...
As Sean Gilbert stepped out of his white GMC pickup, he breathed in the scent of applewood and Columbia Basin dust. Here, just south of Wapato, Wash., one of his 50-acre Gala and Red Delicious apple orchards is ground into huge piles of mulch chips. The wood chipper is the size of a semi-truck and belts out a screeching racket.
He said this ground will lay fallow. It will cost this fifth-generation apple farmer less to leave it unplanted and weedy than to plant another orchard or crop. He scooped up a handful of applewood mulch. "It's a bit of a relief that we're not going to continue to be hemorrhaging dollars on orchards that the market doesn't want," he said. "It hasn't been making sense for a while."
Washington's $9 billion industry grows nearly 70% of the nation's fresh apples, according to Jon DeVaney, president of the Washington State Tree Fruit Association.
DeVaney said farmers are being pressed by the costs of labor, fuel, fertilizer, equipment, as well as weak exports from international tariffs and a strong dollar that diminishes foreign purchasing power.
He estimated thousands of acres of apple orchards across the Northwest are being rapidly torn out, or are not being actively cared for, because many farmers aren't making money growing the fruit. And after several years of similar economic conditions, many farms have gone deep into debt – with even some large, well-established operations filing for bankruptcy.

One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK.
Saurav Das said he was meant to board a flight on Tuesday morning but was told by immigration officers his passport had been "flagged" because of discrepancies involving his date of birth.
In an interview with the BBC, Das said there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on issues that matter to young people.
The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident showed the government was "scared".
"They are scared of the cockroach movement. They're scared of young people asking them questions because they have never had to deal with a generation that wants to ask questions so head on. So that jitters them."
By not allowing him to travel, he said the government had lowered India's stature in the world.
"It's international news that I am unable to travel to the UK," he said. "And this shows Prime Minister Modi in such poor light.
"It's a way to harass, to target activists, young voices in India by the Modi government."
Das said he had been invited by the Oxford Union, as well as universities including Cambridge and Edinburgh, to speak about the movement.

Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.
Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.
In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.
In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.
The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.
Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.
At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.

South Africa convicts Zimbabwean who tried to travel to Russia to fight against Ukraine
A Zimbabwean man has been convicted in South Africa of trying to travel to Russia to fight in its war against UkraineByMOGOMOTSI MAGOME Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 10:50 AM
JOHANNESBURG -- A Zimbabwean man was convicted and sentenced on Tuesday for trying to travel to Russia to fight in its war against Ukraine after being arrested in South Africa with eight others earlier this month.
Tafadzwa Sithole was sentenced to five years in prison, suspended for five years, and he is set to be deported back to Zimbabwe.
He told a South African court that he had agreed to fight for Russia in the war in exchange for “remuneration” after successfully applying online in Zimbabwe.
Sithole said a person he identified as “Albina” contacted him after he submitted the application, arranged accommodation in South Africa and provided a flight ticket to Russia.
His admissions were detailed in a plea agreement with South African prosecutors. He pleaded guilty to violating the Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which prohibits mercenary activity and regulates military assistance to parties in foreign conflicts, including recruitment and training.
The law also applies to foreign nationals.
Sithole, who described himself as an unemployed third-year student at a university in Zimbabwe, appeared in court with four other accused who are also negotiating plea agreements with prosecutors.
He said he entered South Africa legally on Nov. 4 and stayed in accommodation in Kempton Park, east of Johannesburg, in preparation for his travel to Russia.
He was arrested at O.R. Tambo International Airport on Nov. 8 while attempting to board a flight to Russia.

North Korea reviews Switzerland relations after sanctions on youth camp linked to war
North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last monthByKIM TONG-HYUNG Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 2:34 AM
Share
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea threatened Tuesday to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, condemning Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a youth camp in eastern North Korea over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russia-occupied areas of Ukraine.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, described the Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan as an “open hostile act” and a “serious infringement” of the North’s sovereignty, according to a statement carried by state media.
Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials, said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia. She didn't directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated.
North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for economic assistance and military technology transfers.
Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he positions North Korea as part of a united front against the United States.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” North Korean state media said at the time.

A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to NvidiaByLaura BickerChina correspondent Published24 November 2026
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.

The visuals of the historic trilateral meeting may be the only lasting impression left by the summitByAnthony ZurcherNorth America correspondentPublished19 November 2026
Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and he left with little in return.
In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as a historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.
The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting.
